findings.summary: The Adventure Game Interpreter (AGI) is a game engine developed by Sierra On-Line to simplify development of animated, color adventure games. Programmers created a bespoke high-level language (Game Adaptation Language) that compiled into bytecode executed by the interpreter. AGI used vector graphics and off-screen data buffers to conserve disk space and prevent hidden object rendering. It was principally developed for 16-bit home computer architectures and ported to several 8-bit models. After five years and 14 titles, Sierra replaced AGI with the more sophisticated Sierra Creative Interpreter (SCI).

mechanisms.title: Game Adaptation Language compilation
mechanisms.explanation: Programmers created a bespoke high-level language resembling C. A compiler translated this language into bytecode, which was executed by the Adventure Game Interpreter to run games.

mechanisms.title: Off-screen data buffer and bit-block transfer
mechanisms.explanation: Beginning with AGI version 2, graphics were drawn in an off-screen data buffer and then bit-blitted into video memory. This conserved system resources and prevented the game from revealing hidden objects during rendering.
